title: The Pose of Thoughtfulness, or the Unexamined Record of a Faction — On Choi Gyu-seok’s Awl (송곳)
summary: The words of praise that adorn a writer sometimes expose the poverty of the era that summoned him before they reveal his actual achievement.
body: The words of praise that adorn a writer sometimes expose the poverty of the era that summoned him before they reveal his actual achievement. Such is the case with the epithet 'the Korean Ken Loach (K-Ken Loach),' which habitually trailed the name of Choi Gyu-seok. Bestowed upon him merely for the thematic similarity of depicting workers' lives, this unearned crown deserves to be re-pronounced with a colder, more accurate diction. Is he 'K-Ken Loach,' or is he 'K-Cockroach (a play on the Korean version of Ken Loach)'—living as a parasite in the comfortable shade of a political camp while sitting in judgment over others? By retracing his representative work Awl (송곳) and the trajectory before and after it, I intend to show step by step why this rather harsh naming is not mere invective, but a critical thesis.

Let us return first to his point of origin. The decisive turning point that elevated Choi Gyu-seok into the darling of so-called left-wing literary and critical circles was his work twisting the universe of Dooly the Little Dinosaur (whether one calls it a remake or a spin-off, the essence is the same). In the early 2000s, Korean society was passing through an awkward gray zone somewhere between a developing country and an advanced one, both in economic indicators and in civic consciousness. The looseness of an era in which respect for others' creations and intellectual property had not yet settled into universal ethics disguised the act of borrowing another creator's characters as 'socially critical parody' and 'fresh subversion.' Amid the immaturity of an age where borrowing someone else's fictional world easily turned into acclaim once combined with progressive gestures, he effortlessly acquired the status of a 'conscious creator.'

After passing through several political allegories in that manner, what he chose as his debut work on the mass platform of Naver Webtoon was none other than Awl. As is well known, this work takes as its subject the real-life tragedy of the E-Land Homever strike, and borrows the mouth of a character named 'Gu Go-sin'—modeled on labor activist Ha Jong-gang—to preach labor law and the imperative of class struggle. The problem lies in the author's attitude toward real historical events and living human beings.

To appropriate and articulate an acute real-world conflict solely through the narrative of one side is, in itself, an intensely political act. Of course, art can be political. Yet the politics performed by Awl does not advance toward a three-dimensional understanding of the other; instead, it operates by lining characters up toward the predetermined correct answer of a faction. Above all, the point at which this work becomes terrifyingly violent lies in how it treats the people who, despite the story being based on an actual event, could not endure to the end in the ranks of the strike and had to return to their daily lives. Those who halted their strike and returned to the workplace also had livelihoods to sustain, families to support, and existential dread they had to bear as individual human beings. Yet within this narrative serving the grand cause of the camp, their individual circumstances are flattened into cowardice, betrayal, or unenlightened folly.

What makes Awl dangerous is precisely that this violence is wrapped in a 'tone that pretends to be thoughtful.' The author strikes a pose of coolly gazing even upon human ruthlessness or the contradictions within activist circles, yet ultimately that pose is nothing more than a rhetorical alibi designed to defend the moral superiority of his own camp more elaborately. The 'pose' of thoughtfulness must be distinguished from genuine thoughtfulness. Genuine thoughtfulness begins by listening all the way through to the concrete story of each individual who cannot be subsumed under the logic of one's own camp, but Choi Gyu-seok had no intention of doing so from the start—because the stubborn parochialism that 'only our camp is right' had already crushed any curiosity about human beings.

Here we cannot help but ask a question by varying Walter Benjamin's old insight: when the political is aesthetically adorned in order to mobilize emotion, it becomes propaganda rather than art. Why must we call propaganda buried deep in factional logic 'art' and be moved by it? How can a narrative that instrumentalizes human beings as tools of a camp and inflicts literary violence upon the lives of concrete individuals who stepped out of line be ethical? Unquestionably, Awl is a work unworthy of even a single star rating, and insofar as it makes our perception of the world narrower and more ferocious, it is harmful art.

And the finale of this sad comedy is completed in reality outside the work. When an author who had grown and monopolized praise all his life by leaning on factional logic later became an object of denunciation and a 'victim' himself under the blade of solemnism and political correctness within that very camp, the reaction he showed was truly ironic. What does it mean that the follow-up work he released after experiencing his own camp's attacks against him was none other than Hellbound (지옥), a story about the collective madness and lynching of the masses?

What used to be 'righteous class consciousness' when judging others suddenly becomes 'the blind madness of the crowd' when directed at himself. Once he antagonized other camps to claim the moral high ground; now, when people from his own camp curse him, he calls them 'fanatics' and mocks them. Nowhere along this trajectory leading from Awl to Hellbound does there exist any painful self-reflection on the narrow worldview he himself participated in and helped construct. He merely moved from the seat of judging others to the seat of mocking others; the will to look back on the moments when he himself was insensitive to the suffering of others and to renew himself into a better human being is nowhere to be read.

In the end, a writer's ethics is proven not by whom he criticizes, but by how he doubts himself. From the starting line where he became the darling of the era by borrowing another's creation, through Awl, which steamrolled complex human beings at a strike site into flat tools of a camp, all the way to Hellbound, which otherized the public criticizing him as fanatics, Choi Gyu-seok has never once squarely confronted his own arrogance. The monstrous narrative born when one who refuses to listen to the voices of others steps forward claiming to speak for their pain—that is why we must now bid farewell to the deceptive propaganda called Awl.

title: Easy-to-Read Fiction and Half-Baked Whining — On Kim Jiyoung, Born 1982 (82년생 김지영), or the Age of the Victimhood Contest
summary: When evaluating a novel, the phrase 'it reads easily' and the phrase 'it is well written' must be strictly distinguished.
body: When evaluating a novel, the phrase 'it reads easily' and the phrase 'it is well written' must be strictly distinguished. The greatest virtue of Kim Jiyoung, Born 1982 (whether the number in the title is 1982 or 1987, the way this narrative is consumed does not change in the slightest), which is so often praised as a 'well-written novel,' lies strictly speaking not in literary achievement but in its overwhelming 'readability.' It belongs to the exact same genus as the virtue once demonstrated by early Korean internet novels like He Was Cool or Attic Cat—namely, a popular absorptive pull that lets the reader swallow print smoothly without offering the slightest resistance of thought. Yet the flaw of this novel is fatal enough to overwhelm that sole virtue by far; summed up in a single word, it endlessly 'whines.' To put it more precisely, a narcissistic petulance that speaks as though one's own sorrow were the sole and absolute sorrow in the world dominates the entire narrative.

Someone might say: isn't literature ultimately the story of an individual aspiring toward the universal? That is true. However, 'an individual's particular suffering resonating with the lives of others and expanding toward the horizon of the universal' and 'placing my misfortune at the center of the world to force moral indebtedness upon others' are two entirely different things. Let us ask: if there were a world in which the attitude of this novel became universal, what kind of world would that be? Unquestionably, it would be the world of a 'victimhood contest,' where everyone shows off their wounds and competes for supremacy—a world that badgers others by saying, 'I am always the spotless victim, so you who are not must apologize forever,' a perverse world in which the identity of the weak becomes the most potent power to sit in judgment over others.

Before this strange phenomenon, we witness a chilling paradox. Beings who would never have dared utter a sound before the strong if this had been a truly savage world—that is, a raw world governed by physical violence and the law of the jungle—are paradoxically displaying the fiercest bravado within the civilized comfort this society has barely managed to build. Standing atop the very social safety and comfort that gave them a foundation from which to complain safely, they hurl harsh curses at the entire society that cultivated that comfort. Belligerence exercised only within a space where safety is guaranteed is not courage, but pampered petulance; it is not resistance, but reckless bravado.

Let there be no misunderstanding. Literature ought to be able to speak of the pain and sorrow human beings undergo; indeed, it must speak of them. Yet between 'dealing with' suffering and 'wallowing in' suffering lies a world of difference. How on earth can a work that wallows self-pityingly in its own pain and sorrow alone, erasing the complexity of the world, become art? Art should not be a showroom for parading wounds, but an ethical form that asks how a wounded human being nevertheless preserves dignity.

That is why I am genuinely afraid of a landscape in which this world comes to resemble the tone of Kim Jiyoung, Born 1982, filling up to the brim with everyone's half-baked whining. If this is the 'zeitgeist' we have arrived at, nothing could be more dreadful. How dark and suffocating is a world in which a novel absorbed in proving one's own victimhood instead of fathoming the suffering of others—this flat record of petulance—is revered as the bestseller of the age?

Just as the opposite of understanding is not hatred but 'longing'—for we learn longing only before the sublimity of an other whom we cannot fully fathom—on the exact opposite side of where this book stands lies Yiyun Li's Things in Nature Merely Grow. Written from the deepest abyss imaginable to a human being, after losing both of her children to suicide, the attitude of that book stands at the exact antipode of the attitude of 'Kim Jiyoung.' Yiyun Li does not shout at the world to apologize, nor does she privilege her tragedy, nor does she weaponize grief to morally intimidate others. She simply shows the quiet dignity of a human being silently enduring a shattered life, just as things in nature merely grow even amid unbearable pain.

There is unmistakably a stature—a grace of form—both in the way one undergoes suffering and in the way one translates that suffering into sentences. So vast is the distance between half-baked whining and genuine tragic reflection. Therefore, if what you wish to read is true 'art' rather than self-pitying petulance riding on the mood of the era, you should close Kim Jiyoung, Born 1982 and open Yiyun Li's book. That book will prove how literature, instead of making human beings smaller and more neurotic, sustains them as deeper and firmer beings.

title: The Outsourcing of Emotion and the Delivery of Defective Goods — On Lee Won-ha’s Living Alone in Jeju, and I Can’t Hold My Liquor (제주에서 혼자 살고 술은 약해요)
summary: Why borrow the name of the genre called 'poetry' to put into print an impulse that could simply be vented with a single coarse curse and left at that?
body: Why borrow the name of the genre called 'poetry' to put into print an impulse that could simply be vented with a single coarse curse and left at that? And why, before the spectacle of someone jotting down sentences that hardly resemble poetry and posing as a poet, do we as readers feel not merely dismay, but a certain anger? To answer this question, we must first speak of why we read poetry—in other words, what the essence of the tacit 'contract' concluded between poet and reader actually is.

Modern life is grueling, and people lack the time to peer closely into their own inner lives while earning a living and keeping themselves afloat from day to day. That is why we 'outsource' to the specialist called a poet the condensed sensibilities and images we ought to have felt in life, yet failed to feel in time. To have the rightful emotions stolen from us by the speed of the world and the fatigue of living returned at last in the moment we read language exquisitely forged by a poet—that is why we pay the price of a volume of poetry. Yet here is a poetry collection that, far from recovering the emotions stolen from us by the world, desolately strips away even the place of rightful emotion that remained within us. The sigh that never leaves the mind while reading Lee Won-ha's Living Alone in Jeju, and I Can't Hold My Liquor (제주에서 혼자 살고 술은 약해요) is, to borrow Yi Sang-hwa's old line, precisely this: Ah, does spring come even to stolen fields?
Let us read a passage from the collection in concrete detail.

> Hello, sunbae, it is summer here. Whenever this time of year comes around, I miss the memories that used to haunt and pop up. How have you been feeling? I thought we would meet again. I didn't know it would turn out like this. Wherever you are, I hope you're happy. Not long ago a friend betrayed me; she went back to the people who are close to you, sunbae, but used to torment me. Maybe to you I'm no longer a good person, but if I wish for your happiness, do I become a little kinder? Goodbye, and don't be sick, because now you and I can never meet again.
Let us point out on two levels why these sentences cannot be poetry—indeed, why they cannot even qualify as bad prose.

First is the irresponsibility of vocabulary. Consider the phrase, 'I miss the memories that used to haunt and pop up [출몰하던, chulmolhadeon].' The Korean word chulmolhada (出沒하다, to haunt, infest, or appear and vanish suddenly) is used when negative or threatening entities—such as ghosts, bandits, or monsters—abruptly surface and disappear. As a modifier for memories that are the object of longing, this diction is not in the least precise. Of course, someone might invoke 'poetic license' or 'defamiliarization' here. Yet the reader's generosity known as poetic license is a privilege exercised only when that deviation achieves an aesthetic beauty or shudder that surpasses established usage. 'Memories that used to infest/pop up' is neither precise nor lovely enough to warrant the magnanimity of poetic license. It is not a breakthrough chosen after painstaking deliberation, but merely the product of an insensitivity that fails to feel the grain of the mother tongue.

Second is the attitude of the language that follows—namely, crude self-pity. If we strip the quoted lines down to their skeleton, what ultimately remains? 'I thought we would reunite. I didn't know we wouldn't meet. Be happy wherever you are. By the way, someone betrayed me, and I want to look a little nice.' In short, it is an enumeration of clichéd pleasantries and endless whining about private interpersonal relationships. Immature grumblings that ought to be vented in the corner of a diary or a late-night messenger window and promptly deleted pose as poetry solely because line breaks have been inserted.

Let us return once more to the metaphor of 'outsourcing emotion.' If the precious emotions I outsourced to a poet while enduring a harsh life are reconstructed and delivered in nothing more than such imprecise vocabulary and half-baked whining, how is the reader supposed to feel? Unquestionably, it is a breach of contract—a disaster close to making one want to grab the contractor by the collar, shake them, and demand a refund on the spot. When a poet abandons the labor of handling language, the reader receives humiliation instead of recovered emotion.

Lately, inside and outside the publishing world, rumors have circulated that Munhakdongne—long called the stronghold of Korean literature—is in crisis, facing ruin or a possible sale to someone. Of course, publishing this single book of poems is not what tilted that giant publishing house. Yet if a publisher confers the authority of its 'Poets Series' upon a collection of this level, in which not even the minimum apparatus of literary vetting seems to have functioned, and releases it into the world, one must say that the symptoms of its decline were already deeply entrenched within.

Therefore, if someone were trying to acquire that publishing house for a hefty sum at this very juncture, we could not help suspecting one of two possibilities: either they are functionally illiterate when it comes to decoding the language of literature, or else they suffer from a visual and cognitive impairment severe enough to be unable to distinguish a fly buzzing in front of their eyes from a bird soaring through the vault of the sky. Calling a fly a bird does not enable a fly to soar through the firmament of poetry. What Lee Won-ha's poetry collection proves is that sad fact alone.
